events.arc: Single email. emails.job: Get the reader to create one agent, connect their handbook docs, and ask it a real policy question in Slack.
emails.single_idea: The Slack handbook bot you have been scoping is now a configuration job over the docs you already keep — the retrieval layer is part of the platform, not something you stand up.
emails.objection: Standing this up sounds like another integration project — Slack events on one side, a retrieval layer in the middle, a model API on the other, and something to keep working afterwards.
must_not_say: Do not lead on price, free credits, run quotas or plan limits — the competitive read marks these as table stakes and five competitors say them; the free start may be referenced only as the mechanics of the next step, never as the argument.
Do not raise security, compliance, SOC 2, GDPR, encryption or uptime — this reader is not running a vendor review yet, and the field is ahead of us on those axes.
Do not claim or imply SOC 2 certification; it is in progress and not licensed here.
Do not describe retrieval as semantic search, as 'understanding' any phrasing, or as guaranteed to find the right passage — the documented mechanism is top-scoring chunks injected as context.
Do not promise a fixed setup time, a migration time, or that the bot will answer every policy question correctly; propose a first test instead of a result.
Do not assert that the reader has already built, abandoned, or is maintaining an n8n or low-code bot, or that they lost time to one. Any reference to that path must be conditional.
Do not say or imply the agent replaces a backend, a help desk, an internal tools team, or the documentation itself.
Do not name or rank competitors, and do not invent a limitation of other platforms.
No customer names, quotes, logos, counts of users or case studies — none exist.
Do not mention voice, telephony, HIPAA, or industry-specific operational integrations.
Do not pad with the model list, the integration catalogue, guardrails, widgets, white-labelling or analytics features — this email owns one idea.
Banned words per brand voice: solution, synergy, leverage, cutting-edge, revolutionary, game-changing. Also avoid 'introducing' as a headline crutch and any exclamation-mark register.
Do not promise voice or telephony support unless a current licensed source explicitly establishes it.
Do not claim that the agent layer replaces a company's complete backend, product UI, billing, or operational workflow without direct evidence.
Compliance and certification claims are unavailable unless the Evidence Ledger explicitly licenses them.
Do not claim Knowledge base / RAG context; its capability state is unknown.
Do not claim Agent guardrails; its capability state is unknown.
Do not claim Reusable per-client agent configuration; its capability state is unknown.
Do not claim Voice and telephony runtime; its capability state is unsupported.
Do not claim Full SaaS backend replacement; its capability state is unsupported.
Do not claim HIPAA compliance; its capability state is unknown.
Do not claim Deep domain-specific operational integrations; its capability state is unknown.

emails.mechanism: One agent, two connections: Notion syncs page and database content into the agent's knowledge base over OAuth, and Slack installs over OAuth so the bot replies to mentions and channel messages. Between them, the agent pulls the most relevant context for each question itself — there is no vector database to stand up or keep running.

events.subject: A Slack bot that answers from your handbook
events.preview_text: Connect Notion, install Slack, and ask it one real policy question.
events.body:
With orqAgent, a Slack bot that answers policy questions from your handbook is now a configuration job rather than a build.

It is a no-code platform for building AI agents. Create one, connect Notion over OAuth so page and database content syncs into its knowledge base, then install Slack over OAuth — the bot replies to mentions and channel messages.

The reason those questions keep coming back in the channel is that the answer is written down somewhere and hard to reach. Manual retrieval scales with the size of the documentation, not with the question. Past a few hundred pages, that is several searches, or a guess.

There is **no vector database to stand up or keep running**. You upload or sync the documents, and the agent retrieves the most relevant context for every query automatically. That layer is part of the platform, not something you assemble between Slack and a model API.

So the honest first test is small: one agent, your real handbook, and one question a colleague actually asked last week — posted in a channel, answered in front of you.
events.postscript: Starting is free: 1,500 credits on signup, no card required.

events.preview_text: The Slack bot that answers from your Notion handbook is now a configuration, not a build.
events.body:
A policy question lands in the channel. The answer exists — finding it is what takes the time.

So it becomes a manual search: a guess at a keyword, a guess at a page title, then another. That work scales with the size of the handbook, not with the question.

Past a couple of hundred pages, the fallback is guesswork, or a direct ping to whoever keeps the handbook in their head.

orqAgent, a no-code platform for building AI agents, is **available now**. One agent, two connections: Notion syncs your page and database content into the agent's knowledge base over OAuth, and Slack installs over OAuth so the bot replies to mentions and channel messages.

Between them, the agent retrieves the most relevant context for each question automatically — **no vector database to manage**.

Every message it handles in Slack is a real run. It appears in Analytics like an API call, with P95 latency and token usage per model tracked without extra configuration — the record a hand-run search does not keep.

Create one agent, connect the handbook, and ask it a real policy question in Slack.
events.postscript: Signing up takes no card. The free plan starts with 1,500 credits, which is enough to test the bot against real questions.

events.critique_summary: The product is named early and the build-vs-configure argument lands, but the close has to change: it asks for two production OAuth grants and a company-wide verdict off a single test, when E11's upload path and E112's human-in-the-loop default let it ask for something this reader can actually do today.

edits.line: Create one agent, connect the handbook, and ask it one real policy question in a Slack channel.
edits.problem: The first step asks for two production OAuth grants — the company's real Notion handbook and the Slack workspace — to a vendor the reader has never heard of, and all three readers named exactly this as what stops the click ('a bigger ask than one click once real company data and IT approval are involved'). The page offers nothing between reading the email and connecting live HR/policy docs, and E11 licenses a lower-commitment entry the copy never mentions: upload a PDF, doc or plain text.
edits.fix: Narrow the entry point so the reader can watch retrieval work on a document they choose before granting workspace-wide access, with Slack as the second move rather than a precondition. Use only what E11 licenses; do not invent data handling, retention, training or permission-scoping claims — none exist in the ledger.

edits.line: Read what comes back, then decide whether it belongs in front of the whole company.
edits.problem: It escalates a one-question test into a company-wide deployment verdict in the same breath, which is precisely what summons the production-reliability doubt the audience's own sourced context attaches to low-code tooling ('holds up once the whole company depends on it'), and it assumes rollout authority the profile does not establish. Two of three readers cut this line.
edits.fix: Keep the close the size of the test it just proposed. If the email wants to answer the 'what if it answers wrong in front of people' fear, E112 (reply_requires_approval, default ON while testing) is licensed and concrete; the company-wide judgment is not this email's to request.

edits.line: Between them, the agent retrieves the most relevant context for every question automatically — there is no vector database to stand up or keep running.
edits.problem: This is the exact sentence where all three readers stopped. The wording is licensed by E11, so it is not a false claim — the failure is editorial: it is the email's central mechanism claim and it lands as a bare assertion with no concrete follow-up, and to someone weighing policy answers 'for every question' reads as a guarantee of correctness, which the brief explicitly forbids implying.
edits.fix: Keep E11's wording, but pair it with something the reader can check right after it, in the brand's claim-then-literal-follow-up rhythm — what they see when the bot answers, or the human-in-the-loop default. Do not upgrade the claim: no semantic search, no 'understands any phrasing', no promise the right passage is found.

edits.line: NOW AVAILABLE / orqAgent is now available: a no-code platform for building AI agents.
edits.problem: Availability is announced three times — eyebrow, subject/preview framing and body — and the eyebrow buys nothing for a reader scoping a build; one reader cut it outright. The launch itself is supported, the repetition is not doing work and it costs the first line of attention.
edits.fix: State availability once, in the body sentence that also says what the thing is, and let the eyebrow either carry the specific offer or disappear.

edits.problem: The company's sent copy has no captured greeting or sign-off and never signs with a person or a team; 'Hi there' is the generic-blast opener and it pushes the first substantive sentence further down the page.
edits.fix: Open on the first real line the way the sent passages do, and if a sign-off stays keep it plain and in the platform's we/you voice.

events.subject: A handbook bot you can test today
events.preview_text: orqAgent is live: upload one policy document and ask it a question before you connect Slack.
events.body:
Start with one document, not your whole workspace.

orqAgent is now available — a no-code platform for building AI agents. One of them can answer handbook questions in Slack, and you can test it today without connecting either workspace.

Upload a PDF, doc or plain text. The agent retrieves the most relevant context for every query automatically — no vector DB to manage. Ask it the policy question that gets asked most often, and read the answer.

If it holds up, Slack installs over OAuth and the bot replies to mentions and channel messages. Notion connects over OAuth too, syncing page and database content into the knowledge base.

While you test, replies wait for you: **reply_requires_approval is ON by default**. And every message the bot handles in Slack is **a real agent run** — it consumes credits and appears in Analytics exactly like an API call.
events.call_to_action: Create an agent and upload one doc
events.postscript: P.S. No card required to start.
